https://www.dw.com/en/indonesia-dozens-d.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Irh8 The quake caused severe damage to buildings in the area Image: Selo/AFP Advertisement A powerful earthquake struck off the coast of Indonesia early on Saturday, killing at least 47 people and toppling buildings, the National Disaster Mitigation Agency said in its latest statement on Saturday afternoon. The epicenter of the magnitude 7.7 earthquake hit off the coast of the island of Flores at a shallow depth of 10 kilometers (6.2 miles), the US Geological Survey (USGS) said. Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive. Tsunami waves of less than 1 meter (3 feet) were recorded in several areas of the country before the warning was lifted about three hours after the quake. Where did the earthquake strike? Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) recorded the first quake at 4:58 am (2158 GMT) at a depth of 15 km (9 ⁠miles), followed by dozens of aftershocks. People rushed out onto the street as the quake struck Image: Arnold Welianto/AFP Video shared on social media from Maumere, the main town in Sikka Regency on Flores Island in eastern Indonesia, showed part of a building collapsing in a cloud of dust and rubble as people screamed and ran into the street. "Many buildings here were damaged ... I saw that the waiting room at the Pelni port terminal in Maumere had collapsed," Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka, a regency within East Nusa Tenggara province, told AP. Residents evacuated, tsunami warning lifted The initial jolt was followed by a series of aftershocks in the same area, including one of magnitude 6.1. Tourists evacuate after their hotel was severely damaged Image: REUTERS BMKG issued a tsunami warning for part of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, urging residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks. The tsunami warning was later lifted. Rescue workers searching for survivors in the rubble of a destroyed building Image: BASARNAS/AP Photo/picture alliance "We have ended (the tsunami warning) but we will keep monitoring the sea level," Wijayanto, earthquake and tsunami director at BMKG, said. Before the tsunami warning was lifted, residents of Maumere on Flores Island were told to move to higher ground, according to AFP. State television also showed hundreds of people evacuating in nearby Nagekeo regency. Local TV footage showed a hospital in the district of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara Province moving patients outside. Patients and medical staff evacuated from a health center Image: Arnold Welianto/AFP Authorities assessing damage, casualties The quake caused severe damage and collapsed buildings, causing power outages in cities and villages, severely hindering rescue operations. "We are continuing to collect reports of damages and casualties, but there are communication disruptions," East Nusa Tenggara police chief Rudi Darmoko said. Local television reports showed patients at several hospitals being evacuated from buildings as a precaution. "Our students and nuns ran out in panic beneath a collapsing roof," Guidelbertus Tanga, rector of Ritapiret Seminary on Flores said. "At least one priest suffered a broken leg after jumping from the second floor of a building during the quake." There were also damages reported in some part of southern Sulawesi island. Indonesia's history of earthquakes Indonesia is located on the so-called "Ring of Fire," a region of heightened seismic activity in the Pacific basin that stretches from Southeast Asia to Japan. Here are some of the biggest earthquakes to strike the region: 1992, magnitude 7: A tsunami following a strong earthquake on the southeastern island of Flores killed about 2,500 people 2004, magnitude 9.1: A quake struck off the coast of Sumatra triggering a tsunami that killed 170,000 in Indonesia and 220,000 in several countries in the Indian Ocean 2018, magnitude 6.9: A tremor killed more than 550 people on the islands of Lombok and Sumbawa 2018, magnitude 7.5: A quake and a subsequent tsunami in Palu on Sulawesi island left more than 4,300 people dead or missing Edited by: Karl Sexton and Kieran Burke If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google , so you'll always see our verified news first. Photograph: WWL Louisiana New Orleans clergy abuse New Orleans priest accused of abusing children in deaf community dies from apparent fall aged 87 Archdiocese knew of allegations against Gerard Joseph ‘Jerry’ Howell for 40 years but continued to support him Ramon Antonio Vargas and David Hammer of WWL Louisiana in New Orleans Wed 16 Sep 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 06.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A New Orleans Catholic priest whose prolific sexual abuse of children in the local deaf community was known for at least four decades by the city’s archdiocese without meaningful consequence has died after evidently falling in his Texas apartment. Gerard Joseph “Jerry” Howell, 87, was found dead at about 5pm on 8 September by Austin police department officers who were responding to a welfare check on the block listed for the senior living community where he had been residing, the agency said in a statement. The statement – which didn’t name Howell but was provided when police were asked about his death specifically – said first responders had gone to the block to investigate a report that an 87-year-old individual had fallen. Local emergency medical services personnel soon arrived to provide medical aid to that individual, but he stopped breathing and was pronounced dead at the scene, police said. The Austin medical examiner’s office was still working to determine the cause of death in the case on Tuesday, but it was “not being investigated as a homicide”, police said. New Orleans’ Roman Catholic archdiocese provided support to Howell for 40 years after becoming aware of his serial child molestation. They kept him on as an active priest even after reporting him to law enforcement in 1980 and his being publicly exposed by WWL Louisiana in 1992, and then paying him his retirement benefits until at least 2020. A church spokesperson said the archdiocese learned of Howell’s death later that same week. And an archdiocese-managed webpage of dozens of priests and deacons who were removed from ministry for abuse of a minor was then quietly updated to list him as deceased. One of Howell’s most outspoken survivors, Kathleen Austin, said on Tuesday that it was a relief for her to learn of his death. View image in fullscreen Kathleen Austin in God as My Witness. Photograph: Courtesy of filmmakers Lindsay Quinn Pitre and Michael Brandne Sr “He will no longer be able to harm another innocent child,” Austin said. “I can now relax, not worrying about where he is [or] what he’s doing.” Efforts to contact Howell’s family for comment were not immediately successful. Howell’s death is significant because his case was in the public eye for decades while he continued to avoid punishment for abuse he inflicted while ministering to people with impaired hearing. WWL, a Guardian reporting partner, was rolling cameras when Austin confronted him at his home in Texas all the way back in 1992. The news station reported that the archdiocese of New Orleans was aware of many of Howell’s alleged child-abuse victims by then and refused to remove him from active ministry. Records later obtained by the Guardian showed the then New Orleans archbishop, Philip Hannan, reported Howell to the devoutly Catholic district attorney, Harry Connick Sr, in 1980. Connick, though, never charged Howell. Other records showed the next archbishop, Francis Schulte, told Howell to “quit and get a job” after the WWL report in 1992. But Howell appealed to global Catholic leaders at the Vatican, who ordered Schulte to let him “continue as a priest with full financial benefits”. And the records show the New Orleans archdiocese sent Howell for mental health treatment in 2010, with a psychologist diagnosing him as “high risk” and reporting the church was aware of at least 24 child victims. Still, the archdiocese continued to quietly support Howell in his retirement, paying his full living expenses, insurance and a $650 monthly stipend. Those benefits stayed in place until a federal judge halted them in 2020, after the archdiocese filed for federal bankruptcy protection amid the financial fallout of the worldwide, decades-old Catholic clergy sexual molestation scandal. ‘This whole thing’s a farce’: New Orleans Catholic church sex abuse settlement brings anger and shock Read more Yet not even that totally cut Howell off from support by the New Orleans archdiocese. WWL and the Guardian found a 2020 letter that the then New Orleans archbishop, Gregory Aymond, wrote to a Vatican official, calling the bankruptcy court’s cancellation of Howell’s benefits along with those of other archdiocesan clergy abusers “unjust and painful”. The outlets also reported that Aymond had directed Howell to seek aid from a non-profit dedicated to helping priests prohibited from ministering. The leader of that particular group, the Men of Melchizedek, had headed a separate organization which was previously shut down for misusing donations and misleading donors about its purpose. Aymond retired in February and was succeeded as New Orleans archbishop by James Checchio. The archdiocese’s website discloses that Howell, ordained in 1964, was named as the offender in nine claims of sexually abusive or grooming behavior filed as part of its bankruptcy. Immediately before Howell’s death, that was the second most among eight living clergymen on the archdiocese’s list of those removed from ministry for abuse of a minor. About 740 clergy molestation claimants are divvying up a $305m settlement that the archdiocese agreed to pay to resolve its bankruptcy protection case, with individuals’ compensation amounts based on a complicated rubric meant to assess various factors such as the nature and duration of the abuse involved. Many of those claimants name abusers whom the archdiocese has not included in its list of clergy removed from ministry for abuse of a minor. As of the day after Howell’s death, 14 claimants had requested reconsideration of their allocated amounts, and about 220 had indicated they would not contest them, according to a bankruptcy court filing on Monday providing an update on the disbursement of the settlement. The New Orleans archdiocese is among 44 US Catholic religious institutions to have filed for bankruptcy protection in the course of the worldwide church’s clergy abuse scandal – and among 29 to settle such a legal proceeding, according to information compiled by Penn State University’s law school. A spokesperson for the archdiocese said it never restarted Howell’s retirement benefits once they were discontinued, even after the bankruptcy settlement. Howell’s abuse of Austin during her childhood was one of several clergy abuse cases studied by the award-winning 2025 documentary film God As My Witness , which scrutinizes the New Orleans archdiocese’s bankruptcy. For one of the film’s most striking moments, Austin recounts meeting with Hannan to discuss Howell’s abuse of her – only to be directed to “kick him in the balls” the next time she saw him. Austin, who grew up with parents and a sister who were hearing impaired, told film-makers Lindsay Quinn Pitre and Michael Brandner Sr that she was shocked by that guidance. “I remember looking at him thinking, ‘Really? This is how you handle this?’” Austin says in the film , which recently became available on streaming. “‘That’s not my job. This is your job.’” On Tuesday, Austin described having empathy for relatives of Howell, whose late brother and fellow priest Rodney is also considered by church officials to be credibly accused of child molestation. They “had to live with two pedophile priests and the terror that … they inflicted”. Yet Austin added that, to her, Howell’s apparently becoming one of the more than 43,000 people in the US who die from falls annually on average fittingly was “a miserable way to go”. “His death … puts me at rest, and when he meets our maker, hopefully … his punishment far exceeds what he did to children while he was here on the planet,” Austin remarked. Photograph: Lorena Sopena/Reuters Carles Puigdemont Analysis Exiled separatist leader is likely to return to a very different Catalonia Stephen Burgen in Barcelona Nine years on from a failed independence push, former president Carles Puigdemont will find times have changed Mon 5 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 07.51 EDT Share After years of legal wrangling, Spain’s constitutional court is expected to remove the last obstacle to the return of the former Catalan president Carles Puigdemont after nearly nine years in exile this week. Puigdemont fled in 2017 to avoid being jailed for his part in the failed and illegal independence push for which nine of his colleagues were imprisoned on sentences of up to 13 years, although all were released within three years. If on 6 October the court decides, as expected, that the charge of misuse of public funds is covered by the amnesty law passed by the Spanish government in 2024, Puigdemont should be free to return without fear of arrest. But will he come back like Lenin, leaping from the train in St Petersburg to galvanise the faltering revolution, or as yesterday’s man, the last of the Romanovs, bound for the dustbin of history? Whether he returns in triumph or, as he departed, in the boot of a car, Catalonia today is very different from the place he left nine years ago. Firstly, the political climate has changed beyond recognition. The fervour of mass demonstrations and constant conflict and provocation between Barcelona and Madrid has given way to a climate of cooperation. Since 2024, the region has been governed by the Socialists’ party of Catalonia (PSC), the first time since 1980 that a non-nationalist party has been in charge. Led by Salvador Illa, Spain’s health minister during the Covid epidemic, it has ushered in an era of entente with Madrid, where the Socialist Workers’ party, to which the PSC serves as a regional section, is also in the driving seat. Another change is that those young people who got fired up about independence are not only older now but face issues that are more pressing than sovereignty, principally jobs and housing. Wages are low, rents high and mortgages mostly out of reach. As a result, 82% of Catalonia’s 18- to 30-year-olds still live with their parents. On Friday Puigdemont’s Junts per Catalunya (Together for Catalonia) voted down the government’s progressive housing proposals , a move that won’t endear them to young Catalans, nor to their parents. The other big change since 2017 is demographic. When Puigdemont went into exile, 13.8% of the Catalan population was foreign-born; the figure today is 18.7%. This shift is most marked in the capital, Barcelona, where 32% of residents are immigrants representing 118 nationalities, a figure that rises to 50% in the 12-35 age group. For nationalists, this raises the question: who is a Catalan? Jordi Pujol, the Catalan president from 1980 to 2003, insisted that a Catalan was anyone who lived and worked in Catalonia. Things are a little different now. Out of the disillusion of the independence movement has risen Aliança Catalana, a far-right nationalist party whose leader says “there isn’t room for everyone” in Catalonia. Specifically, there would be no room for Muslims, not even those born in Spain, which by implication would include, for example, the Barcelona and Spain football star Lamine Yamal. This has dragged Junts, traditionally the party of the Catalan bourgeoisie, to the right as those on the ethno-nationalist margins gravitate towards the unselfconsciously racist Aliança, whose positions on sovereignty are otherwise barely distinguishable from Junts’. Over the past 25 years, Catalonia, and above all Barcelona, has gone from being a bicultural, bilingual Catalan-Spanish society to one that is multicultural and multilingual. Puigdemont’s pitch is based on identity and a historical sense of grievance at Spain’s perceived abuse of and disdain for Catalonia, a sentiment shared by many, perhaps most, Catalans. This ingrained sense of difference and grievance isn’t going away, but his vision may prove a harder sell than it was 10 years ago. As demography changes, so does identity. Immigrants now make up nearly a fifth of the population, have their own identity issues and have no particular beef with Spain. As for independence, support never did reach 50%, and now hovers in the low 40s. Besides, as people migrate in search of a better or perhaps a more interesting life, it is becoming increasingly likely that the parents of those living in Catalonia will be from different countries, and their sense of national identity is multiple or simply not that important. Puigdemont’s lifelong dream is for Catalonia to take its place among the world’s independent nation states. Yet perhaps he is a man out of time and the nation state he craves, with its monocultural, monolingual badge of identity, has passed its sell-by date. Albert Gea/Reuters INFO A recap of news, sports, lifestyle, entertainment, and human interest images from the Philippines and around the globe MANILA, Philippines — The Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) flagged the financial transactions of Vice President Sara Duterte allegedly related to the flood control issue and illegal drugs, the House prosecution team said on October 5. Based on the summary of reports submitted by the AMLC to the Senate impeachment court, Duterte has 373 covered transaction reports (CTRs) and 34 suspicious transaction reports (STRs), while her husband has 363 CTRs and 30 STRs. When combined, the transactions amount to P4.4 billion. The reports however do not imply that the flagged transactions are illegal, and are part of the monitoring process under the Anti-Money Laundering Act. On October 6, bank representatives took the witness stand to authenticate account records and to verify the accuracy of the veep’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs), which allegedly do not reflect substantial bank balances . On October 7, House prosecutors presented P96 million in manager’s checks as they sought to establish a “pattern of concealment” involving the year-end balances of the Vice President and her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte. Bank of the Philippine Islands officer Marwin Galvez confirmed the father and daughter had a joint time deposit account opened in January 2010 with a principal amount of P40.65 million. Alexander Cabrera, a financial forensic analyst called as a witness, told the impeachment court on October 9 that Vice President Sara Duterte’s undeclared wealth tops P800 million. He said that based on his review of voluminous financial records of Duterte and her husband, Mans Carpio, the couple has around P817 million in undisclosed assets and income from 2022 to 2025.
